newsitem.title: CROATIA: EBRD sees foreign investment boons in E.Europe.
newsitem.headline: EBRD sees foreign investment boons in E.Europe.

text.p: Eastern European countries will provide a wealth of opportunity for investors as countries press ahead with market reforms, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) said on Friday.

As markets grow and become more competitive their contribution to the world economy could grow threefold and their risk is seen as relatively low, EBRD deputy chief economist Ricardo Lago said in an interview.

"It is clearly 'the emerging market' of the 21st century. The important thing is the size of this market and its growth," Lago said during a gathering of international experts on transition economies.

The 26 former communist countries that borrow from the EBRD, with more than 400 million inhabitants, still contribute a meagre part of the global economy. But this is bound to grow as reforms bear fruit, he said.
At current exchange rates, their GDP is estimated to add up to just over $1 trillion out of a global total of $30 trillion.
Lago expects these markets to become more attractive through real growth and increased competitiveness of their goods and services as a result of expected improvements in productivity and quality.

Tighter institutional regulation and fiscal discipline are likely to produce an extra boon as more unrecorded economic activity, suspected to be strong but which is for now escaping the eye of national statistics offices, is netted.

"GDPs can be expected to grow in one decade to $3 trillion at today's prices, which could make the region's GDP almost 10 percent of the world GDP. So emerging market potential for foreign direct investment is threefold," Lago said.
The key question, however, is how to determine the level of risk in order to balance it against what could be a very high return.
Lago believes the risk is not too high although will be built into somewhat higher premiums for some time to come.

"I think the risk of Central and Eastern European countries with future accession to the European Union is low. The experience has shown that these countries keep in general a pretty steady path of reform," he said.
Most countries have seen an upturn after adopting reform policies in key sectors and pressing on with privatisation.
A key theme of the conference has been the large current account deficits which all but three central and east European countries are running -- and whether they are a bad thing.
But Lago described it as "a natural course" for countries importing external capital to supplement scarce domestic savings though, ideally, it should be used to boost productivity.
